title: The Forgotten Aretha Franklin Album That Quietly Changed Music
summary:
You probably know Aretha Franklin as the voice behind "Respect." But tucked away in 1976 is a collaboration that even die-hard fans often overlook: the Sparkle soundtrack. The film itself — a rags-to-riches story about a 1960s girl group loosely based on The Supremes — was only a modest success. Yet its soundtrack, written entirely by Curtis Mayfield and performed by Franklin, is a stunning, risk-taking masterpiece that critics now argue deserves a top spot in pop history.

So why did it slip through the cracks? The album barely cracked the Top 20, and its lead single, the smoldering "Something He Can Feel," stalled at No. 28 on the Billboard pop chart — despite hitting No. 1 on the R&B chart. But chart positions don't tell the whole story. On tracks like "Look into Your Heart," Franklin's voice is a force of nature: tender one moment, explosive the next. The album's peak is the five-minute epic "Hooked on Your Love." It begins as a silky mid-tempo groove, with Franklin gliding over lush strings. Then, around the three-minute mark, she shifts into a raw, gospel-fueled frenzy — shouting, wailing, testifying about love's addictive pull. It's the sound of an artist completely unleashed.

This wasn't just a soundtrack; it was a creative rebirth. The album's influence rippled outward: the 1981 Broadway hit Dreamgirls borrows heavily from Sparkle's plot and style, and a 2012 remake starring Jordin Sparks and Whitney Houston tried to recapture its magic. But nothing matches the original's raw power. As music historian David Ritz once noted, Franklin "poured as much of herself into these Mayfield compositions as she did in the staggeringly great series of hit singles she made for Atlantic Records in the late '60s." So next time you're curating a playlist, skip the obvious hits and cue up Sparkle. It's a buried treasure that still gleams.
why_it_matters: The story of 'Sparkle' proves that commercial success doesn't guarantee legacy. Hidden gems can shape entire genres—a powerful reminder for young listeners to dig deeper than the charts and discover music that might otherwise be forgotten.

background_read: Aretha Franklin (the legendary 'Queen of Soul' who defined R&B with hits like 'Respect' and 'Chain of Fools') was already a superstar by 1976, but the 'Sparkle' soundtrack found her in a creatively adventurous phase.

Curtis Mayfield (the pioneering soul singer and songwriter, famous for the 'Superfly' soundtrack and songs like 'People Get Ready') was a master of social commentary who poured his genius into this project.

The Supremes (the iconic Motown girl group led by Diana Ross) were the loose inspiration for the film's fictional girl group, and their real-life story later fueled the plot of the musical 'Dreamgirls.'
The original 'Sparkle' film was only a modest success in theaters, which partly explains why the soundtrack flew under the radar despite its artistic power.

Streaming has since revived many lost classics; the 2012 remake starring Whitney Houston (in her final film role) attempted to reintroduce the story, but critics still praise the 1976 original as untouchable.

perspectives.description: Music critics and historians view the album as a high point of 1970s soul. Pairing Franklin's voice with Mayfield's songwriting created a sound that was both polished and raw, giving fans a masterclass in vocal emotion.

The album's low chart showing meant it was denied the promotional push it deserved at the time. This reflects a music business that often prioritizes marketability over artistry, leaving brilliant work unheard by wide audiences.

The 'Sparkle' soundtrack illuminates how soundtracks were once a vital creative outlet for major artists—before the era of singles and streaming. It also shows how African American musical innovation has repeatedly been underappreciated in its own time, only to be rediscovered later.

With today's on-demand streaming, buried albums can find new life. Young curators who share playlists online are rewriting history by resurfacing overlooked records like 'Sparkle,' potentially influencing a new wave of artists who prize emotional authenticity over chart formulas.
